summary: At just 1.9 square miles, Lomita packs over 20,000 residents into a density north of 10,700 per square mile — roughly triple the density of the average Los Angeles County suburb — yet it reads more like a quiet grid of single-family blocks than anything approaching an urban core. Wedged between the Palos Verdes Peninsula's coastal hills and the flatter sprawl of Torrance and Harbor City, the city sits close enough to the Pacific that marine-layer mornings are routine, burning off into an annual average of 9.2 sunshine hours per day with highs around 72°F — genuinely mild year-round, with lows rarely dipping below the mid-50s. The housing math is tight: a median home value of $792,100 against a median household income of $92,920 yields a price-to-income ratio above 8.5, making ownership a stretch without significant existing capital, while median rent at $1,918 is more manageable but still claims roughly a quarter of gross household earnings. Pacific Coast Highway slices through town, giving quick access to the harbor and connecting corridors but also fragmenting the walkable fabric. Most employment draws residents outward — aerospace and healthcare employers in neighboring Torrance and El Segundo, the port logistics complex to the south — making this firmly a bedroom community where switching jobs rarely means switching commutes. Lomita's defining tension is geographic: it borrows the Palos Verdes climate and proximity to the coast without the Palos Verdes price tag, but it trades that savings for a compact, highway-bisected footprint with limited local employment.
